speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe the nature of your vertigo and whether it is triggered by specific head movements or positions?

speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you experience any accompanying symptoms such as hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or difficulty with speech or walking? Have you noticed any weakness or numbness on one side of your body?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Gastroenteritis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: The previous diagnosis of gastroenteritis does not explain the vertigo. To differentiate between benign positional vertigo and a central cause like a stroke, I need to know if you have any history of cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, or high cholesterol.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: The patient is otherwise healthy with only a history of eczema. No prior episodes of similar nature. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you have any hearing loss, tinnitus, or a feeling of fullness in one ear? I also need to know if you have any difficulty walking, speaking, or if you noticed any weakness or numbness in your limbs during the episode.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies headaches, hearing loss, tinnitus, loss of consciousness or neurological deficits.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the lack of neurological deficits or auditory symptoms, I suspect Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike maneuver

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Dix-Hallpike Manoeuvre: Positive, inducing nystagmus and reproducing patient’s symptoms of vertigo when head is turned to the left and laid back.

speaker: Doctor
text: The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver confirms a diagnosis of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
